clue.text: Almost no sign of hell in barracks?

parts.note: heck is a mild euphemism for hell

indicators.note: almost means the phrase stops one letter short of its full length

parts.note: no sign of something means you are without it, the suffix -less

explanation.surface: Is a military camp almost free of any trace of hell?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barracks' looks like a noun for soldiers' quarters but is the verb. HECK + LESS gives HECKLESS ('without hell'), and 'Almost' drops its final S.
explanation.definitionFit: To barrack is British for jeering at a speaker, a direct synonym of interrupting with taunts.

clue.text: Warm about right and friendly, ultimately?

definitions.text: Warm about right and friendly, ultimately?

indicators.note: about means placed around the other piece

parts.note: heat is warmth

indicators.note: ultimately means the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone warm on the right lines and friendly in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue serves as definition as well as wordplay: a hearty person is warm and friendly.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearty means warmly cordial and genial, exactly a warm and friendly manner.

clue.text: Gunman's short story for herder

indicators.note: short means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a Colt is a revolver, here the gunman's weapon
a lie is a made-up story

explanation.surface: A Western gunfighter's brief tale for a cowherd.
explanation.definitionFit: The collie is a breed of sheepdog used to herd livestock.

clue.text: Burning to collar first of bullies, one not standing up for Da Ponte, say?

indicators.note: to collar means to grab round, so this word goes around the others

parts.note: lit means burning

indicators.note: first of means the opening letter of the word
in a down clue, up means the word is read upwards, reversed

parts.note: a sitter is someone seated, not standing

explanation.surface: An angry bully is seized, while someone refuses to stand up for an Italian poet.
explanation.walkthrough: SITTER read upward gives RETTIS. Lorenzo Da Ponte wrote the words for Mozart's Figaro and Don Giovanni.
explanation.definitionFit: Da Ponte is a famous example of an opera's wordsmith, who writes the text sung.

clue.text: Case dismissed for dancer's step

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer letters, so those are thrown out

parts.note: Fred Astaire was the famous Hollywood dancer

explanation.surface: A judge throws out a case concerning a dancer's footwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case dismissed' sounds legal; it strips the first and last letters off ASTAIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A stair is a single step in a flight.

clue.text: Depression admitted by nipper after contracting disease

indicators.note: admitted by means taken inside the other piece
contracting means shrinking, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a crab is a creature that nips with its claws
a hole is a depression in the ground

explanation.surface: A child falls into a slump after catching an illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nipper' suggests a small child but means a crab; shortened to CRA, it takes in HOLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Cholera is an acute bacterial infection of the intestine, an example of an illness.

clue.text: Large amounts, a lot moving in pack

indicators.note: in means put inside the other piece

parts.note: a pack is a set of playing cards

indicators.note: moving means the letters shift into a new order

explanation.surface: Plenty being carried, with a lot shifting about in a rucksack.
explanation.definitionFit: Cartloads is used informally for big quantities, literally what a cart holds.

clue.text: Spirit not entirely lifted, oh no!

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted means the letters are read upwards
not entirely means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a spook is a ghost or spirit

explanation.surface: A ghost only half rising, and someone cries out in alarm.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation expresses dismay at a mistake, as 'whoops' does.

clue.text: Illiterate's mark in grotesquely risible book's inscription

indicators.note: in means the cross sits within the jumbled letters of the other word
grotesquely means distorted, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: someone who cannot write signs with a cross

explanation.surface: An unlettered person's scrawl in an absurdly laughable book dedication.
explanation.definitionFit: Ex libris, Latin for 'from the books of', is the ownership label in a volume.

clue.text: Returned with outstanding change of direction, volley initially out

indicators.note: outstanding read as 'standing outside', so this word goes round the rest

parts.note: and means with or together

indicators.note: out means the volley's opening letter is knocked out of the word, as a ball goes out

parts.note: a swerve is a sudden change of direction

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A tennis player hits back, the outstanding swerve making the volley go out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' is not 'excellent' but AND standing outside SWERE (SWERVE minus V).
explanation.definitionFit: Returned can mean replied, as when a remark is returned or answered.

clue.text: Don't plan a German paperback

parts.note: Bild is a German tabloid paper; the 'back' of paperback turns it round

explanation.surface: Advice not to plan, attached to a German paperback book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paperback' must be split: 'paper' gives BILD, and 'back' turns it into DLIB.
explanation.definitionFit: To ad-lib is to improvise, speaking or acting without preparation or a script.

clue.text: Paris cool about attraction of Athens

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Paris shrugs off the appeal of the Greek capital's sights.
explanation.definitionFit: The Acropolis is the ancient citadel above the city, its most famous tourist site.

clue.text: "L'Ogre" by Parisian solver? It's panned!

indicators.note: by means placed next to, so the two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: toi is French for 'you', the solver being addressed
in English 'the ogre', which is the article le plus troll

explanation.surface: A French reader's verdict on a novel called L'Ogre: the critics slated it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panned' reads as savaged by critics, but the definition means kept beside the lavatory pan.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic hint: a lavatory roll hangs beside the pan, so it is 'panned' in a punning sense.

clue.text: Meat cut for queen, say

indicators.note: cut means the word is shortened by its last letter

parts.note: beef is a meat

explanation.surface: A cut of meat suitable for a queen, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' poses as a butcher's term but means chop off the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A queen is one example of the insect, alongside workers and drones in the hive.

clue.text: 19 16, 5 across 12, 1 down 24 and 2 23, loosely speaking?

parts.note: said loosely, the four pairs of linked grid entries sound like horseradish, kohlrabi, artichoke and cauliflower

explanation.surface: A list of cross-references, said casually.
explanation.walkthrough: Say each pair aloud: WHORES REDDITCH, CHOLERA BEE, HEARTY JOKE, COLLIE FLOUR sound like four garden crops.
explanation.definitionFit: Horseradish, kohlrabi, artichoke and cauliflower are all examples of plants grown for the kitchen.

clue.text: End of match lit items, including first leaf

indicators.note: including means the scrambled letters wrap round the other piece
lit is slang for drunk, so these letters are reeling about

parts.note: the first leaf of a document is its top page

explanation.surface: At a match's end, the illuminated things include the opening page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lit' looks like an adjective for items but signals the anagram of ITEMS into S...TIME around TOP PAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoppage time is the period added at the end of a football game for injuries and delays.

clue.text: Legal term tied up in knots, non-U

indicators.note: in knots means tangled, so the letters are mixed up
non-U means without the letter U

explanation.surface: A legal term bound up in knots, and not upper-class either.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-U is British slang for not upper-class; here it just strips U from UP.
explanation.definitionFit: Something permitted is allowed, lawful within the rules.

clue.text: Worcestershire town, flaming dump

parts.note: red describes flames, so flaming means red
to ditch is to dump

explanation.surface: A town in Worcestershire is a blazing rubbish tip.
explanation.walkthrough: Worcestershire is an English county in the West Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Redditch is a town in north Worcestershire, south of Birmingham.

clue.text: Uniform on female, the whole thing in twilight

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above the following piece

parts.note: even means uniform
all means the whole thing

explanation.surface: Uniform worn by a woman, completely, at dusk.
explanation.definitionFit: Evenfall is a poetic word for dusk, the fall of evening.

clue.text: Icon that's silvery peels off

indicators.note: off here means gone bad or awry, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A religious icon whose silver coating is flaking away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Icon' suggests a painted religious image; here it is a pop idol.
explanation.definitionFit: The singer is the archetypal rock-and-roll icon, the King of rock music.

clue.text: Old pros who never tickle colleagues' bottoms

indicators.note: in a down clue, bottoms are the last letters of each word

explanation.surface: Veteran professionals who never pat their colleagues on the behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old pros' suggests veterans; pro is also short for prostitute.
explanation.definitionFit: Pro is slang for a prostitute, so pros here are sex workers in old usage.

clue.text: Cups with vessel, one of a pair in one's cups

definitions.text: one of a pair in one's cups

parts.note: a bra has cups
HMS (His Majesty's Ship) prefixes a naval vessel

explanation.surface: Drinking cups and a ship, while one is drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Brahms and Liszt is Cockney rhyming slang for pissed, drunk; 'in one's cups' also means drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: The composer is half of the rhyming-slang pair meaning tipsy, the state of being in one's cups.

clue.text: Brown finished, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is heard spoken, signalling a word that sounds alike

parts.note: done means finished

explanation.surface: Something brown is complete, so people say.
explanation.definitionFit: Dun is a dull greyish-brown colour, often of horses.

clue.text: Potentially fine to poke nameless cat? That's immature in a bird

indicators.note: to poke means to push into, so this piece goes inside the other
nameless means without N, the abbreviation for name

parts.note: a panther is a big cat

indicators.note: potentially means the letters could become something else, here rearranged

explanation.surface: Could something fine prod a cat that has no name?
explanation.walkthrough: INFE, the anagram of FINE, goes into PATHER, which is PANTHER without its N.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinfeather is a young feather just emerging through the skin, still in its sheath.

clue.text: 0.08 cryptically? That's fine, perhaps

parts.note: 0.08 equals four fiftieths, four over L (the Roman numeral for fifty), so write L breaking into four

explanation.surface: A decimal, oddly, and a shrug that it is acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: L is Roman fifty, and 4/50 = 0.08.
explanation.definitionFit: Milled powder is often fine, so the definition gives an example of something finely ground.

clue.text: Uncle Stalin pinching king's butt

indicators.note: pinching means gripping inside, so it surrounds the other piece

parts.note: Stalin was nicknamed Uncle Joe

explanation.surface: The Soviet dictator nips the monarch's backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A butt is a target of ridicule, a laughing stock.

clue.text: Classic wrong to fear anything from the right

indicators.note: wrong means the letters are put out of order
from the right means the word is read right to left

parts.note: owt is northern English dialect for anything

explanation.surface: It is a mistake to be afraid of anything coming from the political right.
explanation.walkthrough: OWT is Yorkshire and northern English dialect for 'anything'; reversed it gives TWO.
explanation.definitionFit: The song is a much-recorded standard from the musical No, No, Nanette, a classic number.

clue.text: Father having dropped from tree, cutting head on hard wood

indicators.note: on means next to, joining the pieces in sequence
having dropped from means that piece is removed from the other

parts.note: a poplar is a tree
pop is an informal word for father

indicators.note: head means the first letter of the next word

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Dad fell from a tree, then a head-first cut into hardwood.
explanation.walkthrough: POPLAR without POP leaves LAR; 'cutting head' gives C, then H.
explanation.definitionFit: Larch timber is a durable conifer wood used for boats and cladding.

clue.text: Even bits of blubber caught by tough old weapon

indicators.note: caught by means held inside the other piece

parts.note: hard means tough

indicators.note: even bits means the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Pieces of whale fat are trapped by a hardy old weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A halberd is a medieval combined spear and battleaxe on a long pole.

clue.text: In further tests son fights back

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: resits are exams taken again

explanation.surface: A boy rebels while undergoing extra exams.
explanation.definitionFit: To resist is to oppose or withstand an attack, the same as hitting back against it.
